extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting the Alice/Mayo two-part patent-eligibility analysis (Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B) to determine whether claimed subject matter is directed to a judicial exception or contains an inventive concept that renders it patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the judicial exception if it also recites additional element(s) demonstrating that the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One way to demonstrate such integration is when the additional elements apply or use the recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition. Such integration meaningfully limits the claim by going beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment, and thus transforms a claim into patent-eligible subject matter (eligible at Step 2A because not 'directed to' the exception). See Vanda (claims using a law of nature to more safely treat patients were eligible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular treatment or prophylaxis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a 'treatment' or 'prophylaxis' limitation, the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of positive limitations: 'administering amazonic acid to a patient' or 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient.' Anti-examples: intended-use language or field-of-use language (e.g., 'prescribing a topical steroid to a patient with eczema'—not positive because it does not require actual use; 'pharmaceutical composition' or 'feed dispenser is operable to dispense' are not affirmative). Examiners should ensure the limitation actually provides treatment/prophylaxis rather than merely indicating intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor a — Particularity versus generality of treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must be 'particular,' i.e., specifically identified so that it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular example: 'administering a lower than normal dosage of a beta blocker medication to a patient identified as having the poor metabolizer genotype.' Non-particular example: 'administering a suitable medication to a patient' (generic instruction). Examiners may also evaluate related considerations such as 'mere instructions to apply an exception' and 'field of use and technological environment' when determining particularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor b — More-than-nominal relationship to the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim reciting a natural correlation between high blood glucose and ketoacidosis plus 'treating a patient ... with insulin'—insulin materially reduces the risk and thus is significantly related. Counterexample: treating with aspirin (not known to treat ketoacidosis)—only at best a nominal connection and does not integrate the law of nature into a practical application. Examiners may consult considerations such as 'insignificant extra-solution activity' and 'field of use' when analyzing relationship strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor c — Not merely extra-solution activity or field of use
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception and cannot be merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of extra-solution activity: administering vaccines only as a necessary precursor to gather data for a mental analysis step—this does not integrate the exception. By contrast, additionally 'vaccinating a second group ... in accordance with the lowest-risk vaccination schedule' uses the analysis output to change treatment and thus integrates the abstract idea into a practical application. Examiners should consider 'insignificant extra-solution activity' and 'field of use/technological environment' when making determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept principle (Step 2B) — cannot be the judicial exception itself
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive concept 'cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature (or natural phenomenon or abstract idea) itself.' An inventive concept must be an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception that ensures the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'search for an inventive concept' requires identifying claim elements beyond the exception and assessing whether they render the claim 'significantly more.' See Alice and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating whether additional elements amount to an inventive concept requires considering them both individually and in combination to ensure they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because claims must be considered as a whole, an element that is not sufficient alone can contribute to an inventive concept when combined with other claim elements. Examples: Rapid Litigation Management (combination of freezing/thawing steps found non-routine when combined); BASCOM (non-conventional arrangement of generic components).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate inventive-concept search with novelty (§102) or obviousness (§103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although courts often evaluate conventionality of an additional element, the search for an inventive concept is distinct from novelty (§102) and non-obviousness (§103) inquiries and should not be confused with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelty or non-obviousness of an element/step/process is of no relevance to determining whether subject matter falls within §101 categories. Lack of novelty or obviousness does not necessarily indicate that additional elements are not well-understood, routine, conventional elements. See cases cited (Mayo, Diamond v. Diehr, Intellectual Ventures, Synopsys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant consideration i — Improvements to the functioning of a computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that improve computer functioning (e.g., modification of conventional Internet hyperlink protocol to dynamically produce a dual-source hybrid webpage) may qualify as 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See DDR Holdings example; refer to MPEP §2106.05(a) for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant consideration ii — Improvements to other technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that improve technology or a technical field (e.g., modification of rubber-molding process using a thermocouple) may qualify as 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Diamond v. Diehr example; refer to MPEP §2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant consideration iii — Applying the judicial exception with/by a particular machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine (with specific structure arranged in a particular way) can qualify as significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use of a Fourdrinier machine arranged to optimize speed while maintaining quality. See MPEP §2106.05(b) and Eibel Process Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant consideration iv — Effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article
rubrics_metrics.description: A process that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can qualify as significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transforming raw, uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr). See MPEP §2106.05(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant consideration v — Adding a specific limitation beyond routine/conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: non-conventional arrangement of computer components for filtering Internet content (BASCOM). See MPEP §2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant consideration vi — Other meaningful limitations beyond linking to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment may qualify as significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an immunization step that integrates data comparison into a specific immunizing process reducing later disease risk (Classen). See MPEP §2106.05(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-qualifying example i — Adding 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding the words 'apply it' (or equivalent), or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, is not sufficient to provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: indicating an electronic-record-keeping function is performed by a computer (Alice). See MPEP §2106.05(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-qualifying example ii — Appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at a high level
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry, specified at a high level of generality, does not constitute significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims requiring no more than a generic computer to perform generic computer functions (Alice). See MPEP §2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-qualifying example iii — Adding insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (e.g., mere data gathering) is not enough to supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: obtaining information about credit card transactions so that it can be analyzed by an abstract mental process (CyberSource). See MPEP §2106.05(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-qualifying example iv — Generally linking use of the exception to a technological environment or field of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use does not provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: using the abstract idea of hedging in commodities markets (Bilski) or limiting mathematical formula to petrochemical fields (Parker v. Flook). See MPEP §2106.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere physicality/tangibility is not sufficient (and intangibility not fatal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element or elements is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B; a computer's physical existence is not itself an inventive concept. Conversely, presence of a non-physical or intangible additional element does not doom eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit explain that physical implementation alone cannot convert an unpatentable exception into an inventive concept (Alice). Examples: DNA amplification/analysis steps did not provide inventive concept merely because physical (Genetic Techs. v. Merial); improvements not defined by physical components may still be eligible (Enfish, McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: How courts conduct Step 2B analysis (procedural steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts identify additional elements in the claim, consider those additional elements individually (e.g., are they well-understood, routine, conventional?), and then consider them as an ordered combination to determine if the combination adds 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice example: Court identified computer functions/hardware as additional elements, found them individually generic, and found their ordered combination added nothing. BASCOM example: district court identified elements individually as generic but should have considered whether the combination produced a non-conventional, inventive arrangement. Use this three-step approach when conducting the inventive-concept inquiry.
